claims.text: Atomic-scale elemental homogeneity enhances the high-temperature structural stability of near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles.
Atomic-scale elemental homogeneity enhances the high-temperature chemical stability of these nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a single solid-solution phase against intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
Lattice distortion in multi-element alloys lowers atomic diffusivity.
Atomic-scale elemental homogeneity establishes higher diffusion barriers.
Differences in elemental homogeneity translate into differences in lattice strain and diffusion barriers.
Localized elemental enrichment lowers configurational entropy.
Intentional compositional segregation reduces diffusion barriers.
Reduced diffusion barriers in segregated nanoparticles accelerate diffusion-driven phase separation and structural degradation.
Slow cooling and optimized mixing maximize the uniformity of the elemental distribution.
A controlled rapid-cooling protocol can deliberately induce measurable elemental segregation.

Under equivalent annealing, intentionally segregated nanoparticles will show earlier and more pronounced phase separation, secondary-phase formation, or lattice distortion than homogeneous nanoparticles.
Homogeneous multi-element nanoparticles have been documented to retain a single-phase alloy structure during high-temperature annealing.
Ru-5 medium-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remain uniformly dispersed and free of elemental or phase segregation up to 873 K under the reported in situ test.
The proposed homogeneity-controlled mechanism applies throughout 773–1173 K for catalytic operation and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric operation.
Nanoparticle–substrate interactions can govern high-temperature nanoparticle stability and therefore compete with the proposed homogeneity mechanism.
Surface oxidation can dominate degradation and make elemental homogeneity a secondary factor.

Comparable phase stability, lattice integrity, and elemental distributions in the segregated and homogeneous batches under identical annealing conditions would falsify the stated homogeneity mechanism.
